headline: Among the highest-yield counties 43% have lost population, against 4% of the lowest-yield ones
body: Gross rent yield is a year's rent on rented homes divided by the value of owner-occupied homes, so it is highest where homes are cheap. Split the counties of at least 50,000 people into four equal groups by yield, and the typical home is worth $184,300 in the top group, where the typical yield is 5.3%, and $421,600 in the bottom group, where it is 3.3%. The top group also has a higher rental vacancy rate, the share of rental homes standing empty (6.2% against 4.0%), and a higher poverty rate (14.5% against 10.6%). So read a high yield next to rental vacancy and population change, which here is the total between the 2008–12 and 2020–24 surveys, and remember that it leaves out insurance, upkeep and borrowing costs.
sql: WITH c AS (SELECT *, ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY gross_rent_yield DESC, geoid) AS q FROM county_latest WHERE population >= 50000 AND gross_rent_yield IS NOT NULL AND population_growth IS NOT NULL), g AS (SELECT q, median(gross_rent_yield) AS y, avg(CASE WHEN population_growth < 0 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS shrink, median(median_home_value) AS hv, median(rental_vacancy_rate) AS rv, median(poverty_rate) AS pov FROM c GROUP BY q), p AS (SELECT min(trend_from_year) AS y0, max(year) AS y1 FROM c) SELECT 50000 AS min_pop, t.y AS top_yield, b.y AS bottom_yield, t.shrink AS top_shrink, b.shrink AS bottom_shrink, t.hv AS top_value, b.hv AS bottom_value, t.rv AS top_vacancy, b.rv AS bottom_vacancy, t.pov AS top_poverty, b.pov AS bottom_poverty, CAST(p.y0 - 4 AS VARCHAR) || '–' || CAST(p.y0 % 100 AS VARCHAR) AS first_period, CAST(p.y1 - 4 AS VARCHAR) || '–' || CAST(p.y1 % 100 AS VARCHAR) AS last_period, (t.shrink > 2 * b.shrink AND t.hv < b.hv AND t.rv > b.rv AND t.pov > b.pov) AS holds FROM g AS t, g AS b, p WHERE t.q = 1 AND b.q = 4

headline: The owner-occupier tax rate in New Jersey is 6.4× the rate in Hawaii
body: Owner-occupiers pay 1.88% of their homes' value in property tax each year in New Jersey and 0.29% in Hawaii, the highest and lowest rates of any state and more than five times apart. A low rate is not a low bill: homes in Hawaii are expensive, and 20 states have a lower average bill than its $2,901. These are the rates people pay on homes they live in. Landlords and recent buyers often pay more, by an amount that differs from state to state, so this gap does not tell you what a rental home would be charged.
sql: WITH hi AS (SELECT * FROM state_latest ORDER BY effective_tax_rate_agg DESC LIMIT 1), lo AS (SELECT * FROM state_latest ORDER BY effective_tax_rate_agg LIMIT 1), n AS (SELECT count(*) AS cheaper FROM state_latest, lo WHERE state_latest.mean_real_estate_taxes_paid < lo.mean_real_estate_taxes_paid) SELECT hi.name AS hi_state, lo.name AS lo_state, hi.effective_tax_rate_agg AS hi_rate, lo.effective_tax_rate_agg AS lo_rate, hi.effective_tax_rate_agg / lo.effective_tax_rate_agg AS ratio, lo.mean_real_estate_taxes_paid AS lo_bill, n.cheaper AS cheaper_states, (hi.effective_tax_rate_agg > 5 * lo.effective_tax_rate_agg AND n.cheaper >= 2 AND lo.median_home_value > (SELECT median(median_home_value) FROM state_latest)) AS holds FROM hi, lo, n

headline: Inside New York, the owner-occupier tax rate in Monroe County is 4.3× the rate in Kings County
body: Owner-occupiers pay 0.56% of their homes' value a year in Kings County and 2.41% in Monroe County, the widest gap inside any state. Gaps this wide are the exception: 73% of counties have a rate within a fifth of their state's. But in the typical state the highest-rate county still has 1.9× the rate of the lowest, so check the county as well as the state. This covers counties of at least 50,000 people in states with at least 5 of them, and it is the rate owner-occupiers pay, which a landlord or new buyer often does not get.
sql: WITH s AS (SELECT state_name, max(effective_tax_rate_agg) AS hi_rate, min(effective_tax_rate_agg) AS lo_rate, arg_max(county_name, effective_tax_rate_agg) AS hi_county, arg_min(county_name, effective_tax_rate_agg) AS lo_county FROM county_latest WHERE population >= 50000 AND effective_tax_rate_agg IS NOT NULL GROUP BY state_name HAVING count(*) >= 5), m AS (SELECT median(hi_rate / lo_rate) AS typical_ratio FROM s), w AS (SELECT * FROM s ORDER BY hi_rate / lo_rate DESC LIMIT 1), n AS (SELECT avg(CASE WHEN abs(c.effective_tax_rate_agg / st.effective_tax_rate_agg - 1) <= 0.2 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS within_fifth FROM county_latest c JOIN state_latest st USING (state_fips) WHERE c.population >= 50000 AND c.effective_tax_rate_agg IS NOT NULL AND c.state_name IN (SELECT state_name FROM s)) SELECT w.state_name AS state, w.hi_county, w.lo_county, w.hi_rate, w.lo_rate, w.hi_rate / w.lo_rate AS ratio, m.typical_ratio, n.within_fifth, 50000 AS min_pop, 5 AS min_counties, 15 AS top_states, (w.hi_rate / w.lo_rate > 2 AND m.typical_ratio >= 1.5 AND n.within_fifth > 0.5) AS holds FROM w, m, n

headline: 19 of the 50 counties with the highest owner-occupier tax bills are also among the 50 with the highest tax rates
body: Rate and bill go together, but not closely. The bill is the rate multiplied by what homes are worth, so an expensive county can have a low rate and a large bill: 9 of the 50 highest-bill counties have a rate below the middle of all 999 counties of at least 50,000 people. Of those, Marin County, California has the largest bill: owner-occupiers there pay an average of $14,323 a year at a rate of 0.77%, below the middle rate of 0.83%, in a county where the typical home is worth $1,507,300. 7 of these low-rate, high-bill counties are in California, where a home's taxable value is reset when it is sold, so a buyer would pay a higher rate than the one shown. Both figures describe long-standing owner-occupiers, not new buyers or landlords.
sql: WITH c AS (SELECT *, rank() OVER (ORDER BY mean_real_estate_taxes_paid DESC) AS rb, rank() OVER (ORDER BY effective_tax_rate_agg DESC) AS rr, median(effective_tax_rate_agg) OVER () AS med FROM county_latest WHERE population >= 50000 AND effective_tax_rate_agg IS NOT NULL AND mean_real_estate_taxes_paid IS NOT NULL), e AS (SELECT * FROM c WHERE effective_tax_rate_agg < med ORDER BY rb LIMIT 1), k AS (SELECT count(*) AS n, count(*) FILTER (WHERE rb <= 50 AND rr <= 50) AS both_top, count(*) FILTER (WHERE rb <= 50 AND effective_tax_rate_agg < med) AS low_rate, count(*) FILTER (WHERE rb <= 50 AND effective_tax_rate_agg < med AND state_name = 'California') AS low_ca FROM c) SELECT 50 AS top_n, 50000 AS min_pop, k.n, k.both_top AS both, k.low_rate, k.low_ca AS low_state_count, e.name AS ex_name, e.mean_real_estate_taxes_paid AS ex_bill, e.effective_tax_rate_agg AS ex_rate, e.med AS median_rate, e.median_home_value AS ex_value, (k.both_top < 25 AND k.both_top > 5 AND k.low_rate >= 2 AND 2 * k.low_ca > k.low_rate AND e.rb <= 50) AS holds FROM k, e

headline: 100 counties account for about half of the new homes permitted in the country
body: Those are the 100 counties that permitted the most homes from 2020 to 2024, out of 3,035 with permit records. They account for 50% of the homes permitted and hold 33% of the homes that already exist, so building is more concentrated than housing itself. Texas and Florida alone account for 28% of permits and 16% of existing homes. Permits show where building is happening; they follow demand at least as much as local rules, so they do not show where rules are loose or strict.
sql: WITH c AS (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY permits_per_year DESC, geoid) AS rn FROM county_latest WHERE permits_per_year IS NOT NULL AND housing_units IS NOT NULL), k AS (SELECT count(*) AS n, sum(permits_per_year) AS permits, sum(housing_units) AS homes, sum(permits_per_year) FILTER (WHERE rn <= 100) AS top_permits, sum(housing_units) FILTER (WHERE rn <= 100) AS top_homes FROM c), s AS (SELECT state_name, sum(permits_per_year) AS permits, sum(housing_units) AS homes, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY sum(permits_per_year) DESC) AS sr FROM c GROUP BY state_name), s2 AS (SELECT max(state_name) FILTER (WHERE sr = 1) AS state_1, max(state_name) FILTER (WHERE sr = 2) AS state_2, sum(permits) AS permits, sum(homes) AS homes FROM s WHERE sr <= 2) SELECT 100 AS top_n, (SELECT max(year) - 4 FROM c) AS first_year, (SELECT max(year) FROM c) AS last_year, k.n, k.top_permits / k.permits AS permit_share, k.top_homes / k.homes AS home_share, s2.state_1, s2.state_2, s2.permits / k.permits AS state_permit_share, s2.homes / k.homes AS state_home_share, (k.top_permits / k.permits BETWEEN 0.45 AND 0.55 AND k.top_permits / k.permits > 1.25 * k.top_homes / k.homes AND s2.permits / k.permits > 1.25 * s2.homes / k.homes) AS holds FROM k, s2

headline: The fastest-growing counties permit new homes at 7.0× the rate of the counties that grew least
body: Split the counties of at least 50,000 people into four equal groups by population growth. The fastest-growing group permits 21.3 new homes a year for every 1,000 existing homes. The group that grew least, 82% of which lost people, permits 3.1, and the figure falls at each step in between. Counties that gained people are also the ones building, which is close to unavoidable, since newcomers need homes. So a county with few permits may have few people wanting to move in, or may allow too little building for them to do so; the number cannot tell these apart, and says nothing on its own about how strict its building rules are. Population growth is the total between the 2008–12 and 2020–24 surveys, a longer stretch than the recent years the permit figures cover.
sql: WITH c AS (SELECT *, ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY population_growth DESC, geoid) AS q FROM county_latest WHERE population >= 50000 AND population_growth IS NOT NULL AND permits_per_1000_units IS NOT NULL), g AS (SELECT median(permits_per_1000_units) FILTER (WHERE q = 1) AS p1, median(permits_per_1000_units) FILTER (WHERE q = 2) AS p2, median(permits_per_1000_units) FILTER (WHERE q = 3) AS p3, median(permits_per_1000_units) FILTER (WHERE q = 4) AS p4, avg(CASE WHEN population_growth < 0 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) FILTER (WHERE q = 4) AS shrank4, min(trend_from_year) AS y0, max(year) AS y1 FROM c) SELECT 50000 AS min_pop, 1000 AS per, p1 AS top_permits, p4 AS bottom_permits, shrank4 AS bottom_shrank, p1 / p4 AS ratio, CAST(y0 - 4 AS VARCHAR) || '–' || CAST(y0 % 100 AS VARCHAR) AS first_period, CAST(y1 - 4 AS VARCHAR) || '–' || CAST(y1 % 100 AS VARCHAR) AS last_period, (shrank4 > 0.5 AND p1 > 2 * p4 AND p1 > p2 AND p2 > p3 AND p3 > p4) AS holds FROM g

headline: Since 2008–12, home values have risen 19% after inflation in the middle county, rents 8% and household incomes 8%
body: These are total changes between the 2008–12 and 2020–24 surveys, counting each county of at least 50,000 people once, whatever its size. Home values grew faster than incomes in 79% of these counties, so in most of them homes cost more years of income than they did. Rents, measured with utilities included, kept pace with incomes in the middle county, but large counties differ: the counties where rents outgrew incomes hold 73% of the people. Keep the starting point in mind: the first period includes the housing bust, when prices were unusually low, so part of the rise in values is a recovery. Each figure is also a five-year average and lags today's prices and rents.
sql: WITH c AS (SELECT * FROM county_latest WHERE population >= 50000 AND real_home_value_growth IS NOT NULL AND real_rent_growth IS NOT NULL AND real_income_growth IS NOT NULL), k AS (SELECT median(real_home_value_growth) AS v, median(real_rent_growth) AS r, median(real_income_growth) AS i, avg(CASE WHEN real_home_value_growth > real_income_growth THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS share, sum(population) FILTER (WHERE real_rent_growth > real_income_growth) / sum(population) AS rent_pop, min(trend_from_year) AS y0, max(year) AS y1 FROM c) SELECT 50000 AS min_pop, v AS value_growth, r AS rent_growth, i AS income_growth, share AS value_beat_income, rent_pop AS rent_beat_income_pop, CAST(y0 - 4 AS VARCHAR) || '–' || CAST(y0 % 100 AS VARCHAR) AS first_period, CAST(y1 - 4 AS VARCHAR) || '–' || CAST(y1 % 100 AS VARCHAR) AS last_period, (v > r + 0.05 AND v > i + 0.05 AND abs(r - i) < 0.03 AND r > 0 AND i > 0 AND share > 0.5 AND rent_pop > 0.5) AS holds FROM k

headline: Since 2008–12 the owner-occupier tax rate has fallen in 77% of counties, and in 73% of those the tax bill still rose after inflation
body: The rate is tax paid divided by home value, so it falls whenever home values rise faster than tax bills, even if the bills go up. In the typical county the average owner-occupier bill rose 10% after inflation between the 2008–12 and 2020–24 surveys, while the typical home value rose 19%. A falling rate on a county's trend chart is therefore not a sign that owners there pay less. This covers counties of at least 50,000 people, and describes what owner-occupiers pay; the first period includes the housing bust, when home values were unusually low.
sql: WITH c AS (SELECT l.*, t.effective_tax_rate_agg AS first_rate FROM county_latest AS l JOIN county_trend AS t ON t.geoid = l.geoid AND t.year = l.trend_from_year WHERE l.population >= 50000 AND l.real_tax_growth IS NOT NULL AND l.real_home_value_growth IS NOT NULL AND l.effective_tax_rate_agg IS NOT NULL AND t.effective_tax_rate_agg IS NOT NULL), k AS (SELECT avg(CASE WHEN effective_tax_rate_agg < first_rate THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS rate_fell, avg(CASE WHEN real_tax_growth > 0 THEN 1.0 END) FILTER (WHERE effective_tax_rate_agg < first_rate) AS n_up, count(*) FILTER (WHERE effective_tax_rate_agg < first_rate) AS n_fell, count(*) FILTER (WHERE effective_tax_rate_agg < first_rate AND real_tax_growth > 0) AS n_both, median(real_tax_growth) AS bill_growth, median(real_home_value_growth) AS value_growth, min(trend_from_year) AS y0, max(year) AS y1 FROM c) SELECT 50000 AS min_pop, rate_fell, CAST(n_both AS DOUBLE) / n_fell AS bill_up_given_fell, bill_growth, value_growth, CAST(y0 - 4 AS VARCHAR) || '–' || CAST(y0 % 100 AS VARCHAR) AS first_period, CAST(y1 - 4 AS VARCHAR) || '–' || CAST(y1 % 100 AS VARCHAR) AS last_period, (rate_fell > 0.5 AND CAST(n_both AS DOUBLE) / n_fell > 0.5 AND bill_growth > 0 AND bill_growth < value_growth) AS holds FROM k
